analysis.one_liner: Bars the use of mining and other waste to fill in streams and rivers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 131 cosponsors in the House, was referred to a subcommittee in April 2011 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Clean Water Act's definition of "fill material" so that waste could no longer be legally dumped into rivers and streams under a fill permit. Its main target is the practice of mountaintop-removal coal mining, in which mining companies blow off mountaintops and push the leftover rock and soil—the waste—into adjacent valleys, burying streams. Under current rules, that waste can be permitted as "fill"; this bill would exclude any pollutant discharged into water primarily to dispose of waste. The bill never advanced: it was sent to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then its Water Resources subcommittee, and died there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near mountaintop-removal coal mines in Appalachia, whose streams and drinking-water sources are contaminated by mining waste, and downstream communities that draw water from those waterways. The bill gives regulators clear legal authority to deny permits that bury streams with mine waste.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Clean Water Act to define "fill material" as any pollutant that replaces waters of the United States with dry land or changes a water body's bottom elevation, but excludes "any pollutant discharged into the water primarily to dispose of waste." [S2] [S3]

Under that definition, waste dumped into streams—such as the rock and debris left over from mountaintop-removal mining—could no longer be permitted as "fill," closing the legal route companies use to bury streams. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining companies operating surface mines in Appalachia, which would lose the ability to dispose of mining waste by dumping it into valleys and streams, and would face higher waste-handling costs and potentially fewer permitted mines.

drawbacks.text: Restricting waste disposal in streams would raise the cost of surface coal mining in Appalachia, and opponents of such measures have argued this threatens mining jobs in a region with few alternative employers.

Because the definition covers any waste discharged into water, the bill could complicate other activities—such as some construction or dredging projects—that currently dispose of material in waterways under fill permits, beyond its intended target. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give people living near mountaintop-removal mines clear federal protection for their streams and drinking water, at the cost of higher waste-disposal expenses for the coal industry and pressure on mining employment in parts of Appalachia. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how one weighs permanent water contamination against jobs in a struggling region; the bill itself took no position on compensating miners, which is its most serious design gap. The mechanism, however, is narrow and targeted: it changes one definition in existing law rather than creating a new regulatory regime.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the 112th Congress without a hearing, a vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ) introduced the Clean Water Protection Act on April 5, 2011, with more than 50 original cosponsors listed at introduction. [S3]
The bill attracted 131 cosponsors—129 Democrats and 2 Republicans—roughly 30% of the House. [S4]
It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on the day of introduction, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment. [S5]

No further action appears in the record: the subcommittee held no markup or vote, the full committee took no action, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mining companies are better off, because the existing rules allowing mining waste to be permitted as stream "fill" remain in place. Residents near mountaintop-removal mines gain nothing, since the protections the bill offered never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal companies; stream protections never happened

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Water Protection Act on April 5, 2011, to exclude waste from the Clean Water Act's definition of fill material.

for.name: 131 House members
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, 129 Democrats and 2 Republicans, roughly 30% of the chamber.

against.name: Rep. John Mica
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; the record shows no markup, hearing, or vote after referral.

against.name: Coal mining industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation restricting the disposal of mining waste in streams, which would have ended the practice of using waste fills in mountaintop-removal mining.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic—129 Democrats to 2 Republicans—and with Republicans holding the House majority and the committee chairmanship in the 112th Congress, the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the industry's practice of disposing of mining waste by dumping it into valleys and streams under fill permits, protecting nearby communities' water at the industry's expense. Because the bill died, the industry's existing disposal method remains intact.
